summary:
EarthToMars Analog Atlas is an interactive, space-themed web map that helps identify and characterize Earth locations that serve as analogs for permanent Moon bases and Mars exploration sites. Users choose a lunar or Martian target, weight six dimensions (geology, thermal extremes, ice and water, dust and wind, subsurface caves, terrain), and get a ranked list of Earth analogs, including lesser-known sites such as the Lut Desert, Danakil Depression and Lanzarote lava tubes.

The tool addresses the challenge by explaining what makes each site analogous, where the analogy breaks down, and how it could support exploration, while noting Earth’s limits in gravity, vacuum, atmosphere and radiation. It uses NASA GIBS, Solar System Treks and the NASA POWER API, and includes a trend-analysis tab with regression, Sen’s slope and Mann-Kendall significance testing.

It matters because no single Earth site matches the Moon or Mars. A transparent, multi-dimensional comparison helps teams choose better test sites, find overlooked locations, and make planetary analog science accessible to students and the public.
details:
What it does and how it works

EarthToMars Analog Atlas is an interactive, space-themed map for finding Earth locations that act as analogs for permanent Moon bases and Mars exploration sites. You pick a target (Shackleton Rim and Marius Hills lava tubes on the Moon, Jezero Crater and Arcadia Planitia on Mars) and weight six dimensions: geology and materials, thermal extremes, ice and water, dust and wind, subsurface and caves, and terrain and operations. The app ranks twelve Earth sites by similarity. These include famous ones such as the Atacama and Haughton Crater, and lesser-known ones such as the Lut Desert, Danakil Depression, Lanzarote lava tubes and Tibesti.

For each site it shows where the analogy is strong, where it breaks down, and how the site could support exploration. It also states Earth’s limits: reduced gravity, vacuum, thin atmosphere and radiation. A “Data Detective” tab pulls live annual climate data from NASA POWER for the selected site. It plots the series and runs linear regression, Sen’s slope and the Mann-Kendall test to say whether a trend is statistically significant.

Benefits

The tool treats an analog as a set of matches and mismatches rather than one place that “looks like Mars”. Mission planners, students and educators can compare sites on the dimensions that matter to them. Because it runs in a browser with no install, it is easy to use and share.

Intended impact

We want to make analog-site selection more systematic, draw attention to under-studied locations, and teach the public to read satellite data critically. The same method could later be scaled to a global, raster-based search.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript, with Leaflet for mapping
  • NASA GIBS (MODIS imagery) for Earth
  • NASA Solar System Treks (LRO and MOLA) for the Moon and Mars
  • NASA POWER API for climate time series
  • NASA APOD API
  • Google Fonts (Orbitron and Inter)
  • Python and reportlab for the presentation
  • AI assistance (Claude) for code and drafting, which should be disclosed in line with the event’s AI rules

Creativity

  • A weighted similarity metric that users control
  • Explicit “where the analogy breaks down” analysis
  • Lesser-known analogs alongside famous ones
  • A single mission-control interface that moves between Earth, the Moon and Mars
  • Statistical trend testing built into the same tool

Factors considered

  • No Earth site matches every condition, so the app scores several dimensions instead of ranking by overall appearance.
  • Scientific honesty: the site profiles are currently curated estimates from the literature, not values computed from rasters. We plan to replace them with LOLA, MOLA, THEMIS, MODIS and SRTM-derived values.
  • Trend analysis is linear and uses annual means, which removes seasonality but ignores autocorrelation.
  • Accessibility, with a responsive layout for phones and desktops.
  • Reliability, because Moon and Mars tile endpoints may change.
